title: Symmetric Encryption
summary: Block and stream ciphers, AES at a conceptual level, and the modes of operation — ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM — that determine whether an encryption scheme actually holds up, or leaks structure the moment it's used wrong.

slides.markdown:
AES is the encryption algorithm underneath nearly everything — TLS, disk encryption, encrypted messaging. But "we use AES" is an incomplete sentence: **AES alone doesn't specify how to encrypt more than one 128-bit block**, and the answer to that question — the *mode of operation* — is where most real-world symmetric encryption failures actually happen, not in AES itself.

This topic covers the cipher (block vs stream, AES conceptually) and then spends most of its depth on modes, because that's the part interviewers probe and the part engineers get wrong in practice: ECB's structural leak, CBC's padding-oracle history, CTR's stream conversion, and GCM's authenticated encryption — plus the single mistake (nonce reuse) that breaks several of them at once.

A **block cipher** encrypts data in fixed-size chunks — AES operates on 128-bit (16-byte) blocks, always. Data that isn't an exact multiple of the block size needs padding, and data longer than one block needs a *mode of operation* to chain blocks together sensibly (the next several slides).

A **stream cipher** encrypts data one bit or byte at a time, generating a pseudorandom keystream from the key (and a nonce) and XOR-ing it against the plaintext as it flows — no padding, no fixed chunk size. ChaCha20 is the modern standard example, popular in mobile and low-power contexts because it's fast in software without needing dedicated hardware acceleration the way AES benefits from.

The line between them blurs in practice: several of AES's own modes (CTR, GCM) turn the block cipher into something that behaves exactly like a stream cipher, generating a keystream instead of directly encrypting each block. That convergence is exactly why the *mode* matters as much as the underlying cipher choice — you can turn a block cipher into a stream cipher, but only if you pick the mode that does it safely.

**AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)** won a public, multi-year NIST competition in 2001 and has been the world's default symmetric cipher since — a direct payoff of the open-design principle from [Cryptography Foundations](crypto-foundations).

The shape, conceptually rather than bit-by-bit: AES always operates on **128-bit blocks**, regardless of key size. The key size — **128, 192, or 256 bits** — determines how many transformation **rounds** the cipher runs (10, 12, or 14 respectively), where each round mixes the block through substitution and permutation steps designed so that flipping a single input bit changes roughly half the output bits, unpredictably. More rounds means more accumulated mixing, which is why larger keys aren't just "harder to brute-force" but also run more rounds of diffusion.

For almost every practical purpose today, **AES-128 is fully secure** — the key length analysis from Cryptography Foundations already covers why brute force is hopeless at that size. AES-256 is chosen for extra margin (compliance requirements, or hedging against future cryptanalytic or quantum advances) rather than because AES-128 has any known weakness.

slides.subTitle: Why the mode matters as much as the cipher
slides.markdown:
AES specifies how to scramble one 16-byte block given a key. It says nothing about what to do with the second block, the third, or the ten-thousandth — that's the job of a **mode of operation**, and choosing the wrong one produces a scheme that's cryptographically broken even though the underlying AES implementation is flawless.

This is a genuinely common real-world failure mode, not a theoretical one: a developer calls `AES.encrypt(data, key)` in a library that defaults to a specific mode without the developer ever consciously choosing it, ships it, and has unknowingly picked the least secure option available. The cipher was never the weak point — the *mode* was.

The rest of this topic walks four modes in the order most engineers actually encounter them: ECB (the trap), CBC (the historically dominant but flawed default), CTR (a clean stream-cipher conversion), and GCM (the modern recommended default, combining encryption with built-in integrity).

slides.subTitle: Why identical blocks leak a pattern
slides.markdown:
**ECB (Electronic Codebook)** is the simplest possible mode: encrypt each 16-byte block independently, with the same key, no interaction between blocks. It's also the mode you should almost never use, for exactly the reason its simplicity implies.

Because each block is encrypted identically and independently, **identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks.** If a 16-byte region repeats in the input — a large area of solid color in an image, a repeated field in structured data — that repetition survives, visibly, in the ciphertext. The data is technically "encrypted" and yet its structure leaks straight through.

ECB is genuinely still the *default* mode in some older libraries and tutorials, which is why it keeps showing up in real audits despite being a textbook example of what not to do. The fix is never "use ECB carefully" — there's no careful way to use it for data with any repeating structure, which describes almost all real-world data.

![A blocky plaintext pattern stays visible when encrypted block-by-block under ECB, but disappears into noise under CBC](assets/ecb-vs-cbc-blocks.svg)

This is the classic "ECB penguin" style demonstration: encrypt an image with a repeated-block structure under ECB and its outline still shows through, because identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks. Encrypt the same image under CBC and the result is uniform noise. The exact same key, the exact same cipher, and the exact same plaintext produce a result that either completely leaks the image's shape (ECB) or looks like pure noise (CBC), purely because of how blocks relate to each other. "It's AES-encrypted" told you nothing about which of these two outcomes you got.

slides.subTitle: Chaining, IVs, and the padding-oracle risk
slides.markdown:
**CBC (Cipher Block Chaining)** fixes ECB's repetition leak by XOR-ing each plaintext block with the *previous* ciphertext block before encrypting it — so identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext, because each one's encryption now depends on everything before it in the message.

The first block has no predecessor, so CBC needs an **initialization vector (IV)** — a random value XORed with the first plaintext block instead. The IV doesn't need to be secret, but it must be **unpredictable and never reused** with the same key (more on why in the pitfall slide ahead).

CBC's well-known historical weakness is the **padding-oracle attack**: CBC requires padding to fill the last block, and if a system reveals — even indirectly, through a timing difference or a distinct error message — whether decrypted padding was valid, an attacker can use that single bit of feedback, repeated thousands of times, to decrypt an entire ciphertext without ever knowing the key. This is precisely why unauthenticated CBC (no integrity check on top) is considered risky today, and why GCM, which builds integrity in, is the modern recommendation instead.

slides.subTitle: Turning a block cipher into a stream cipher
slides.markdown:
**CTR (Counter mode)** takes a completely different approach: instead of encrypting the plaintext directly, it encrypts a **counter** (a nonce combined with a block index) to produce a keystream, then XORs that keystream against the plaintext — exactly the shape of a stream cipher, built from a block cipher.

This gives CTR two practical advantages CBC doesn't have: blocks can be encrypted and decrypted **in parallel**, since each block's keystream only depends on its counter value, not on any previous ciphertext; and it needs **no padding**, since XOR works on any length of data, not just full blocks.

The catch, and it's a serious one: CTR's security depends entirely on **never reusing the same counter value with the same key**. If it happens, two different plaintexts get XORed with the *same* keystream segment, and XORing the two resulting ciphertexts together cancels the keystream out entirely, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts — from which both can often be recovered with basic cryptanalysis. This is the general nonce-reuse problem covered in the pitfall slide, and CTR is one of the modes most sensitive to it.

slides.subTitle: In a single pass
slides.markdown:
**GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)** is CTR mode's encryption, plus a built-in authentication tag computed alongside it — giving you confidentiality *and* integrity from one primitive, in one pass over the data, without needing a separate HMAC step glued on afterward.

This matters because "encrypt, then separately authenticate" is a place engineers historically got the *order* wrong — authenticating plaintext and then encrypting it, or worse, doing only one of the two — and each ordering mistake has its own subtle vulnerability. GCM removes that decision entirely: call one function, get ciphertext plus a tag, and verification fails loudly on any tampering rather than silently decrypting corrupted or attacker-modified data.

This is why GCM (written as **AES-256-GCM** in practice) is the modern default recommendation across TLS 1.3, most new application-level encryption, and the answer to "what should I use" absent a specific reason to choose otherwise. Its one sharp edge is the same nonce-reuse sensitivity as CTR, inherited directly from CTR's counter-based construction — get nonce handling right and GCM is close to a solved problem for symmetric encryption.

slides.sectionTitle: ECB vs CBC vs CTR vs GCM
slides.markdown:
| | ECB | CBC | CTR | GCM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Leaks repeated blocks?** | Yes — the core flaw | No | No | No |
| **Needs padding?** | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| **Parallelizable?** | Yes (but irrelevant given the flaw) | No (chained) | Yes | Yes |
| **Built-in integrity?** | No | No | No | Yes |
| **Nonce/IV reuse risk** | N/A (broken regardless) | Predictable IV weakens it | Catastrophic — cancels keystream | Catastrophic — same as CTR, plus breaks authentication |
| **Recommended today** | Never | Only with a separate MAC, and mostly legacy | Fine, but rarely chosen over GCM | Yes — the default choice |

The practical takeaway for almost any new system: **use GCM.** It gets you past ECB's structural leak, avoids CBC's padding-oracle history, and bundles the integrity check CTR alone doesn't provide — one mode that resolves nearly every mistake on this row by row, provided nonce management (next slide) is handled correctly.

slides.sectionTitle: Reusing an IV or nonce with the same key
slides.markdown:
The single mistake that breaks CTR, GCM, and weakens CBC, all at once: **reusing the same IV/nonce with the same key.**

For CTR and GCM, reuse means two different messages get XORed with the identical keystream segment — XOR the two ciphertexts together and the keystream cancels out, leaving the XOR of the plaintexts, which is often enough to recover both messages with straightforward analysis. For GCM specifically, nonce reuse additionally breaks the authentication guarantee, potentially letting an attacker forge valid-looking tags. For CBC, a predictable (though not necessarily reused) IV enables a different class of attack that can leak information about the first plaintext block.

This has happened in production: several real-world systems have shipped with a fixed or predictable nonce — a counter that resets on restart, an all-zero IV used as a "simplification," a nonce derived from a low-entropy source — and each is a version of this exact mistake. The fix is mechanical: generate nonces with a cryptographically secure random source (or a counter that's guaranteed globally unique and never resets across the key's lifetime), and never hardcode or default one to a fixed value.

The practical decision tree for almost every new system, distilled from everything above: default to **AES-256-GCM** (or ChaCha20-Poly1305, the stream-cipher equivalent, when hardware AES acceleration isn't available). Generate a fresh, random nonce per message using a cryptographically secure random source, and never let a nonce repeat under the same key. Never use ECB. Treat unauthenticated CBC as a legacy pattern to migrate away from, not a new default.

The senior-level nuance interviewers listen for: knowing GCM's default status isn't a rule to recite blindly — it's a rule that follows directly from ECB's structural leak, CBC's historical padding-oracle exposure, and CTR's missing integrity check, all being solved simultaneously by one construction. Being able to explain *why* GCM wins, not just that it does, is what separates "I looked this up" from "I understand cryptographic engineering."

The next topic, Asymmetric (Public-Key) Cryptography, picks up the other half of the pipeline from Cryptography Foundations — the key-pair side that solves the problem symmetric encryption alone can't: how two parties agree on the very key this whole topic assumed they already had.
